en: The Blessed Lord said: They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below.
The Vedas are its leaves; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda. //1//
Śrīdhara:
Without dispassion, there is neither knowledge nor devotion; therefore, it is clear that the Lord taught in the fifteenth chapter that knowledge must be refined by dispassion.

In the passage beginning with "He who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion at the end of the previous chapter" (Gītā 14.26), it was stated that for one who worships the Supreme Lord with exclusive devotion, the state of Brahman arises through the knowledge obtained by His grace.
Since neither exclusive devotion nor such knowledge is possible for one who is not dispassionate, [the Lord], desiring to teach knowledge preceded by dispassion, says:
First of all, describing the nature of saṃsāra through the poetic ornament of a tree metaphor in two and a half verses, the Blessed One said: "With roots above" (ūrdhvamūlam).
"Above" means supreme; it refers to that which has the Puruṣottama as its root—the one who is superior to both the perishable and the imperishable.
The word *adhaḥ* (below) refers to those conditioned by their functions who exist prior to that [Brahman], such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others.

They call Him the *aśvattha* because they are like branches (*śākhā*) of Him; and because, being perishable, He will not remain even until tomorrow morning, He is unfit to be relied upon, and thus is called *aśvattha*.
And because it is uninterrupted in the form of a continuous flow, they call it imperishable (*avyaya*).
Such are the scriptural passages beginning with: "This eternal *aśvattha* tree has its roots above and its branches below" (KaṭhU 2.3.1).

The Vedas are its leaves; for, by means of establishing dharma and adharma, the Vedas—standing in the place of leaves—are shown to be that upon which all living beings depend, through the fruits of action which stand in the place of shade for the tree of saṃsāra. He who knows such a fig tree as this is indeed a knower of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Lord (Īśvara) is the root of the tree of the manifold proliferation of saṃsāra;
Brahmā and the others are his portions, standing in the place of the branches. And that tree of saṃsāra is perishable.
It is also eternal in the form of a continuous flow, and it has been rendered as something to be cultivated through the rituals prescribed in the Vedas; indeed, this alone is the meaning of the Veda.
For this very reason, one who knows thus is praised as a "knower of the Veda. //1//
Madhusūdana:

In the preceding chapter, the Blessed One, having explained the *guṇas* as the causes of bondage to *saṃsāra*, stated that liberation—the state of being Brahman—is attained through devotion to Me by transcending them:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion... (18.55).
"Having transcended these qualities, he is fit for becoming Brahman" (Gītā 14.26).

In this regard, to address the doubt—namely, how a human being such as yourself can attain the state of Brahman through the yoga of devotion—the Blessed One spoke this verse, which serves as a foundational aphorism (sūtra) to reveal His own nature as Brahman: "For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable."
"And [he attains] the eternal Dharma and absolute bliss" (Gītā 14.27).
This fifteenth chapter is now commenced as a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon this aphorism (*sūtra*),
explaining how a person, having realized the true nature of the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa and becoming transcendent of the *guṇas* through the worship of love for Him, may attain the state of Brahman.

Having heard the Lord’s words beginning with "I am indeed the foundation of Brahmā," and perceiving Arjuna to be overcome by wonder— thinking, "How can this man, who is my equal, speak thus"— and being unable to ask anything due to both fear and shame, the Blessed Lord, desiring out of compassion to reveal His own true nature, spoke the verse beginning with "ūrdhva."

In this regard, since only one who has become detached from worldly existence (saṃsāra) is qualified for the knowledge of the reality of the Blessed Lord and not otherwise— as was stated in the previous chapter—
the Lord now describes saṃsāra, which is the effect of the conjunction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa under the control of the Supreme Lord, by way of the metaphor of a tree;
this is done for the sake of generating detachment, as that [tree] serves as the means for transcending the Guṇas which is the subject at hand.

"Urdhva" means the supreme root or cause; it is Brahman, because its nature is self-luminous, supreme bliss, and eternity. Therefore, "urdhva" refers to that which remains unsublated even when all of saṃsāra is sublated, being the substratum for the delusion of all saṃsāra. That very Brahman is the root of this [tree] through Māyā; thus, it is "ūrdhva-mūla" (upward-rooted). By "adhas" (below), the downward-turned limiting adjuncts (*upādhis*) consisting of effects—such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others—are understood.

Because its branches extend in various directions, it is "branching" (śākhā); because it perishes quickly, it is unworthy of trust, as it will not remain even until tomorrow—thus it is the "aśvattha. The Śrutis and Smṛtis declare this illusory tree of saṃsāra to be "imperishable" (avyaya), for it is the substratum for the beginningless and endless continuum of bodies and so forth; they declare self-knowledge to be infinite and imperishable.
First, the scriptural passages (śruti) are those recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, beginning with: "This eternal aśvattha tree has its roots above and its branches below" (KaṭhU 2.3.1).

The term *arvāk-śākha*—meaning "having branches directed downwards"—is synonymous with the phrase "having downward-reaching branches" (*adhaḥ-śākha*); it signifies that its branches, such as the intellect (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are inferior and characterized by their effects, extend downwards.
The word *sanātana* is synonymous with the term *avyaya* (imperishable).
And the Smṛtis state:
"The tree of worldly existence has the Unmanifest as its root and source; it arises from the grace of that very [Lord];
it consists of the trunk of the intellect and has the sense organs as its hollows."
The great elements are its branches, and it possesses leaves through the sense objects;
it has the flowers of merit and demerit, and yields the fruit of pleasure and pain.
The eternal tree of Brahman is the means of subsistence for all beings;
this is its forest of Brahman, and within it, Brahman moves like a witness.
Having cut through and shattered this with the supreme sword of knowledge,
and having thereby attained the state of the Self, one does not return from there again.
[And so forth.
"The Unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to Brahman characterized by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Māyā; that very thing is the root cause. He whose origin is from that is "born therefrom.
Having arisen and grown through the grace of that very root, the Unmanifest, because of its extreme firmness.

For just as the branches of a tree arise from its trunk, so too do the various transformations of saṃsāra arise from the intellect (*buddhi*). By virtue of this similarity, the intellect alone is the "trunk"; this [world] consists of it and is abundant with it.
He whose inner spaces—the gaps between the sense faculties—are his hollows;
he whose various branches are the great elements beginning with space and ending with earth, or he whose trunk is the "viśākha" (the forked one);
he who is the means of subsistence, that which is lived upon.
The "Brahma-tree" (*brahma-vṛkṣa*) is the tree presided over by Brahmā, the Supreme Self;
it is eternal because it cannot be cut down without the knowledge of the Self.

This is the "Brahma-forest" (*brahma-vana*); it is a forest because it is to be enjoyed, desired, and cultivated by this Brahmā in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), and thus Brahmā acts like a witness within it.
But the meaning is that one is not tainted by what has been done.

Having cut and split this "forest of Brahman," which consists of the tree of saṃsāra—with the sword of extremely firm knowledge that "I am Brahman"—having severed it along with its roots; having attained the goal which is the nature of the Self, one does not return from that liberation which is the nature of the Self. This is the meaning.

The rest is clear. Here, this poetic construction (*rūpaka-kalpanā*) should be understood as comparing [the subject] to a great *aśvattha* tree that is being pushed by the waves of the Gaṅgā, which has fallen obliquely onto its high bank, and which has been half-uprooted by the wind, yet remains alive.
Therefore, there is no inconsistency in its having roots above and branches below.

Of this *aśvattha* tree composed of *māyā*, the Vedic hymns—characterized as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*—are like leaves; for they are "leaves" (*parṇāni*) because they conceal (*cchādanāt*), that is, they veil the reality of the true essence, or because they protect the tree of *saṃsāra* through the ritual sections (*karma-kāṇḍa*).

Just as leaves serve to protect a tree, so do the ritual sections (*karma-kāṇḍa*) serve to protect the tree of *saṃsāra*, because they have the purpose of illuminating dharma and adharma, along with their causes and effects.

He who knows—that is, understands—that aforementioned *aśvattha* tree of *saṃsāra*, which consists of illusion and has roots, he alone is a knower of the Veda; the meaning is that he alone is a knower of the meaning of the Veda, which comprises both action (*karman*) and Brahman.
Indeed, the root of the tree of saṃsāra is Brahman, while the individual souls (jīvas), beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha, occupy the place of its branches.
Furthermore, that tree of saṃsāra is perishable in its essential nature, yet it is infinite in the form of its continuous flow.
It is watered by the rituals prescribed in the Vedas and cut down by the knowledge of Brahman; for this alone is the meaning of the Veda.
He who knows the meaning of the Veda is indeed all-knowing; thus, he praises the knowledge of the tree together with its root as "one who knows the Veda. //1//
Viśvanātha:

"The cutter of the cycle of worldly existence, unattached, a portion of the Lord of the Self, superior to both the perishable and the imperishable—the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa"; such is the narrative in the fifteenth [chapter].
In the preceding chapter:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman."
Thus it has been said.
To the question, "In that case, how can you, who are a human being, attain the state of Brahman through the yoga of devotion?

the answer is: It is true that I am indeed a human being, yet I am the foundation and the supreme refuge even of that Brahman; with this in mind, this fifteenth chapter, which serves as a commentary (*vṛtti*) upon this aphorism-like statement, is now commenced.

Regarding that which was stated, "having transcended the qualities" (*tatra sa guṇān samatītya*), one might ask: what is this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the qualities, or from where has it proceeded? Furthermore, who is the individual soul (*jīva*) that, by devotion to Him, transcends transmigratory existence; and as for what was stated, "he is fit for becoming Brahman" (*brahma-bhūyāya kalpate*), what indeed is Brahman?

In response to the inquiry, "Are you the support of Brahmā, or who are you? and so forth, [the Lord] first describes this wondrous cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) as the *aśvattha* tree by means of the poetic figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

He describes it as having its single root in the form of the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), which is the first sprout arising from the seed of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), located above—in the world of truth (*satya-loka*) at the summit of all worlds;
and as having infinite [branches] below, in the realms of heaven (*svarga*), the intermediate space (*bhuvar*), and the earth (*bhūr*).

That whose branches are the gods, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Asuras, Rākṣasas, Pretas, Bhūtas, humans, cattle, horses, and other animals, birds, worms, insects, moths, and stationary beings—that is the Aśvattha, the supreme tree, so called because it accomplishes the four aims of life beginning with Dharma.
By way of word-play (śleṣa), for those possessed of devotion, it is "Aśvattha" in the sense that it will not stand until tomorrow; the meaning is that it is as good as lost.
But for those who are not devotees, it is imperishable and immutable.

The Vedas— such as "One desiring offspring should offer a white animal to Vāyu, and one desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra"— which enjoin ritual actions, are like leaves because they cause the increase of *saṃsāra*.
For a tree is made beautiful by its leaves;
he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
And thus says the Kaṭha-vallī Śruti: "This eternal Aśvattha has its roots above and its branches below" (KaṭhU 2.3.1). //1//
Baladeva:
"Dispassion that cuts through worldly existence, the eternal individual soul who is my portion,
and I, the glorious one who am supreme over all"— this is recorded in the fifteenth [chapter].

In the preceding section, it was stated that although the individual soul (jīva) possesses the eight innate qualities such as consciousness and bliss, it experiences attachment to the qualities of material nature (prakṛti-guṇa) through the will of the Lord in accordance with its beginningless karmic impressions (vāsanā). This attachment is manifold, and its cessation occurs through discriminative knowledge headed by devotion to the Lord. When that occurs, the soul, having attained its own true nature, takes refuge in the Lord and remains forever established in Him in a state of supreme joy.

Now, in this fifteenth chapter, detachment (*vairāgya*)—which establishes the steadiness of the knowledge that discriminates [the Self] from that [world]—is described for the sake of its application to the matters already mentioned: namely, the individual soul’s status as a portion of the worshipful Lord and the Lord’s supremacy over all others.

In this regard, since the world composed of the *guṇas* is the object of detachment, the Blessed One describes it by figuratively representing the world as a tree and detachment as a weapon: "With roots above... (*ūrdhvamūlam*).
By these three [verses] beginning with "ity ādi," they describe the *aśvattha* tree that is the nature of *saṃsāra* as having its roots above and its branches below.

Its root is above— in the world of truth (*satyaloka*) at the very summit— consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), which takes the form of the four-faced Brahmā, appearing as the first sprout arising from the primary seed.

Below Satyaloka, in the worlds of Svar, Bhuvar, and Bhūr, it has branches extending in various directions consisting of gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, beasts, birds, insects, moths,
and down to stationary objects;
because it is the support for the fruits of the four aims of life, it is the supreme tree, the Aśvattha.

Without such discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), there can be no cessation [of suffering]; therefore, it is imperishable (*avyaya*) and eternal (*nitya*) by way of its continuous flow. Regarding this, the Śruti says:
"Rooted above, with branches below... (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 6.1).
This is the eternal Aśvattha tree;
he who truly knows this tree as having its roots above and its branches below.

[KaṭhU 2.3.1] These are the opening words. Of this *saṃsāra*-tree, they say that the *chandas*—the Vedic statements that teach what is action and what is inaction—are the leaves, because they nourish its root, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Those *chandas* are as follows: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu; [one should offer] an eleven-fold oblation to Indra... and so forth.
One should understand such passages as "one desiring offspring should offer [the sacrifice]," and so forth.
A tree grows and flourishes by means of its leaves; he who knows that *aśvattha* tree as it has been described—that is, who understands it—is truly a knower of the Veda (*veda-vit*).
Indeed, the Veda speaks of the world as a tree with the intention that it must be cut down; the meaning is that one who knows the means for cutting it down is a knower of the Veda's true purpose.
Its branches, nourished by the gunas and having sense-objects as their sprouts, extend downward and upward.
And below, their roots extend downward, following after karma in the world of humans. //2//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and below":
the individual souls (jīvas) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who have the conditioned effects [of karma] as their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), are said to occupy the position of the branches.
Among them, those who are evildoers extend downward into the wombs of animals and so forth; they are the branches of that tree of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, they have grown—that is, attained increase—by means of the qualities (*guṇas*), such as the functions of *sattva* and the rest, like the watering of water.
Moreover, their "sprouts" (*pravālas*) are the sense-objects (*viṣayas*), such as form and so forth;
this is because they are joined with the activities of the senses (*indriya-vṛttis*), which occupy the position of the tips of the branches.
Furthermore, by the word "and" (ca), it is implied both below and above;
the roots are spread out and grown.
The primary root is the Lord (Īśvara) himself.
These intermediate roots, however, are characterized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for various enjoyments.
Regarding their effect, it is said that "in the world of humans they are followed by karma";
that is, those whose subsequent sequence consists of karma itself arising in future times.

Indeed, for those who have reached the human world upon the exhaustion of their karma due to the impressions (*vāsanā*) of various enjoyments experienced in the higher and lower worlds, there occurs an engagement in various corresponding actions;
for it is only in that [human] world that there is authority over karma, and not in other worlds.
Therefore, it is called the "human world. //2//
Madhusūdana:
Another conceptualization concerning the constituent parts of that very tree of transmigratory existence is stated in the verse beginning with "Below...
(adhaś ca). Previously, individual souls (jīvas) whose limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are effects—such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others—were described as being in the position of the branches.
Now, however, the specific distinction pertaining to that is stated:
among them, those of foul conduct who have performed evil deeds have spread downward, extending into the wombs of animals and so forth;
whereas those of pleasant conduct who have performed good deeds have spread upward into the wombs of gods and so forth, and from there, downward into the state of humanity.
Starting from Viriñca (Brahmā) and extending upward from him as far as Satyaloka, the branches of that tree of saṃsāra have spread forth.
Of what nature are they?

They have grown and become gross through the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which—having transformed into the forms of the body, the senses, and their objects—act like the watering of a tree.

Furthermore, the objects such as sound and so forth are like the sprouts upon those branches of the tree of *saṃsāra*; thus, they are so described because of their connection with the functions of the senses, which occupy the position of the tips of the branches, and because they serve as the locus for passion (*rāga*).
Because it is conjoined [with them].

Furthermore, both below—and by the word "ca" (and), also above—the roots, which consist of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and so forth produced by various enjoyments, are like roots that cause the activity of merit and demerit; they are continuously extended and interwoven throughout that tree of saṃsāra.
And since Brahman alone is the primary root, there is no fault.
Of what nature are the intermediate roots?
They are "karmānubandhīni," meaning those whose nature (*śīla*) is to produce subsequent consequences (*anubandha*), namely actions characterized by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

Where? In the human world (*manuṣya-loka*). This "human world" refers to the body qualified by [castes] such as Brahminhood; therein, [the karmas] are for the most part connected to action (*karma-anubandhin*).
For it is well known that humans alone possess the qualification for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*). //2//
Viśvanātha:

Below, in the wombs of animals and so forth, and above, in the wombs of gods and so forth, the branches of that tree of saṃsāra have spread out and grown through its qualities—the functions of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*—like the watering of water.
Those [branches] which have sense objects, such as sound and the rest, as their sprouts—that is, those for which the objects occupy the position of young shoots—are such.
Furthermore, it is inferred that at its root there exists some great treasure-store unperceived by all the worlds;
for even though that Aśvattha tree stands supported by the roots of its own base, like a Baṭa tree, it possesses external aerial roots upon its branches as well— thus he says, "And below."
Even for that [existence] which has its root in the Brahma-world, roots connected with and dependent upon karma continue uninterruptedly and extensively below it in the human world.
The meaning is that because of these fruits of karma, at the end of their enjoyment, one again becomes engaged in karmas specifically within a human birth. //2//
Baladeva: Furthermore, as for the phrase "and below":
the branches of that tree of worldly existence (saṃsāra), which has been described by its characteristics, extend both downward and upward.
They extend downward into the wombs of humans, animals, and so forth, due to evil deeds; and they extend upward into the wombs of gods, gandharvas, and so forth, due to good deeds.

The sense objects— sound, touch, and so forth— are the sprouts (*pravāla*) of these [trees], having grown through the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the others, which act like the sprinkling of water, and thus possessing bulk. Because they are connected with the functions of the ears and other senses— which occupy the position of the tips of the branches— and because sound and the other objects are the substrata of passion, they occupy the position of the sprouts.
Beneath that *aśvattha* tree, as well as above and in between, there are subsidiary roots that extend and spread out.

These, consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth produced by various enjoyments, are called "roots" because they cause one to engage in righteous and unrighteous actions (*dharma-adharma*).
The primary root is the four-faced Brahmā; such [root], while the various latent impressions are the subsidiary roots, like the masses of interwoven aerial roots of a banyan tree—this is the sense.

As to what those [actions] are like, he says: they are connected with karma in the human world; because, when the experience of the fruits of karma has come to an end here and there, they become once again the causes of karma in the human world.
Indeed, that world is well known as the "field of karma. //2//
Its form is not perceived here in such a way;
it has neither end, nor beginning, nor any established foundation.
Having cut down this *aśvattha* tree with its deeply rooted roots using a firm, unswerving sword, //3//
Therefore, that goal should be sought after,
reaching which they do not return again;
to that very Primal Person, I take refuge.
From which the ancient course of worldly activity has proceeded. //4//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore,

"nor its form" means that by living beings situated here in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the form of this tree of saṃsāra— characterized by such features as having its roots above— is not perceived.
And there is no end or termination because it is inexhaustible;
nor is there a beginning because it is beginningless;
nor is there a foundation or stability.
"How does it stand?"—this cannot be perceived.

Since this tree of saṃsāra is thus difficult to cut down and productive of misfortune, one should therefore sever it with the firm weapon of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and strive for the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). Thus he says, "This aśvattha... in the verse consisting of one and a half lines.

Having cut down— having severed and separated— this Aśvattha tree, which has deeply rooted roots and is firmly established in its foundation, by means of that firm weapon which is non-attachment (asaṅga)— that is, freedom from attachment consisting in the renunciation of the notions of "I" and "mine"— [one must transcend it]. //3//

"From that": from that [state], one must thoroughly search for—that is, investigate—that state which is its fundamental basis. Of what nature is it? It is that state having reached which, once attained, they do not return; the meaning is that they do not turn back.
He explains the very manner of this investigation with the words "that very same."

Since this ancient, long-standing activity of saṃsāra has spread and expanded, I take refuge in—that is, I go for shelter to—that very same primordial Person. This means that He is to be sought with such one-pointed devotion. //4//
Madhusūdana:

As for this tree of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-vṛkṣa*) described here, its form— such as its having roots above and so forth— is not perceived by living beings dwelling in this world in that manner, just like a dream, a mirage, water [in a desert], an illusion, or a city of the Gandharvas.
Because its nature is seen to be false and subject to destruction,
its end or conclusion is not perceived;
for it will never reach completion within this much time, as it is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, its beginning is not perceived;
because it has proceeded from this point onward, it is without beginning.
Nor is its foundation—its middle state—perceived.

Because it has beginningless and endless correlates, this tree of worldly existence (saṃsāra-vṛkṣa) is thus difficult to cut down and the cause of all misfortune; therefore, with the weapon of non-attachment (*asaṅga-śastra*), one must cut down the aforementioned *aśvattha* tree, whose roots are deeply established and firmly bound by beginningless ignorance (*anādy-ajñāna*). [The word] "attachment" (*saṅga*)...

Attachment to desire is the opposite of non-attachment; renunciation consists in the abandonment of the longing for son, wealth, and the worlds. That very thing is the weapon, because it opposes the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) composed of passion and hatred.
By means of that firm weapon of non-attachment—strengthened by the yearning for knowledge of the Supreme Self and sharpened by repeated practice of discernment—[one should cut through attachment].
Having cut [the bonds] and uprooted them by means of the perfection of dispassion, tranquility, self-control, and so forth, one performs the renunciation of all karma; this is what is meant. //3//

Then, having approached the Guru, that Vaiṣṇava state situated above the Aśvattha tree must be thoroughly sought—that is, it must be searched for and investigated—according to the Śruti: "He is to be sought; He is to be desired to be known. The meaning is that that state is to be known through hearing (śravaṇa) and the other [means of knowledge].
What is that state (*pada*) into which those who have gone, having entered by means of knowledge, do not return—that is, they do not turn back again toward *saṃsāra*?
How is that to be sought?
To this he says: [seek] that very first (*ādya*), primordial Person (*puruṣa*) who exists at the beginning, by whom all this [was created], who is expressed by the word "state" (*pada*).
"I take refuge in Him who lies within the city or within the bodies"—this is the meaning: that He is to be sought as one's sole refuge by thus going for shelter with single-minded devotion.
Which person? [He is the one described as follows:]...

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: from which Person (*puruṣa*) this ancient, beginningless, and long-standing activity—the unfolding of the tree of *māyā*-based transmigratory existence—has issued forth, like illusory elephants and the like from a magician; that Person one should take refuge in. //4//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, in this world of humans, his form—his essential nature—is not perceived with certainty; the sense is that this is due to the diversity of the doctrines of various disputants, such as "this is real," "this is false," or "this is eternal.
Nor has he an end because he is infinite, nor a beginning because he is beginningless, nor a foundation or support.
The sense is that its support or even its nature cannot be apprehended due to the absence of knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*).

Let this tree be as it may; having known the unattached sword that cuts this tree—which is the sole cause of the suffering of all living beings—one must cut it down and seek the great treasure situated at its very root.
Thus he says: "the Aśvattha."

Having severed with that weapon—the axe of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), which means detachment from everything—and having thereby separated [the self] from itself, one must then search for that state, the reality which is its very root, in the form of a great treasure:
Brahman.
Of what nature is it? To this he says: "that state reached by which, having gone, they do not return," meaning they do not come back again.
He describes the manner of seeking:

"I take refuge in—that is, I worship with devotion—that very primordial Person from whom this ancient, long-standing activity of saṃsāra has spread and expanded. This is the meaning of what is to be sought. //3-4//
Baladeva: Its form—that is, the form of this Aśvattha tree—is not perceived here in the world of men in the manner I have described, characterized by having its roots upward and so forth.
Nor is its end or destruction perceived.
How this mass of evils, so entangled, could perish is not known.
Furthermore, no initial cause for this is perceived;
from where has such a thing as this arisen?
Nor is its foundation or support perceived.
"What is the basis upon which this person persists? [He replies:
"But I am a human being, the son of Yajñadatta and the father of Devadatta."
The meaning is that one who performs actions corresponding to those [past deeds] is known only as "happy" or "unhappy," or "I dwell in this region, in this village"— nothing more.

Since this *aśvattha* tree is thus difficult to understand and is the cause for this vow toward what is not the ultimate good (*anartha*), therefore, by means of the knowledge of the true nature of reality obtained through association with the virtuous (*sat-prasaṅga*), one should [cut it down].

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "having severed [the bond] with the weapon of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), the firm axe of dispassion (*vairāgya*) sharpened by the practice of discrimination (*viveka*), and having separated it from itself, that state (*pada*) is to be thoroughly sought.
Attachment (*saṅga*) is the longing for sense objects; its opposite is non-attachment, which is dispassion (*vairāgya*).
That very weapon, because it destroys the desire for that [tree], has its roots deeply established—that is, its roots are utterly firm according to the manner previously described.

Therefore, that state situated above the root of the *aśvattha* tree of saṃsāra must be sought; it is to be investigated by means of the practices such as hearing (śravaṇa) obtained through devotion to Me.
As to what that state is like, He says: "In which... (yasmin).
Once people have gone there by those means, they do not return from that place, just as one does not fall back from heaven.
He speaks of that very method of seeking,
for from it this ancient, long-standing activity of the world has spread and expanded.
The seeking of Him is described as being preceded by *prapatti*—the thought, "I take refuge in that very Primal Person"—through such means as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

For He alone is the cause of the universe, and through birth from Him comes the cessation of *saṃsāra*; indeed, He is Kṛṣṇa Himself, as stated in passages such as, "I am the source of all," and "This divine energy consisting of the modes... and so on.
And because [the object] is manifested by the statement beginning with "it does not illuminate that," etc. (3-4).
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the inner self, and with desires turned away;
Freed from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, those who are undeluded go to that imperishable state. //5//
Śrīdhara: Showing other means for attaining that [state], he says "nirmāna... and so forth.
Those from whom pride (*māna*) and delusion (*moha*)—namely, egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and false attachment (*mithyābhiniveśa*)—have departed;
those by whom the fault consisting of attachment to sons and the like has been conquered.
They are eternally established in the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma-ātma-jñāna*).
Those from whom desire has especially ceased are [the ones referred to].
Because they are the causes of pleasure and pain, cold, heat, and so forth are called "pairs" (*dvandva*) and designated as "pleasure and pain."
Released by them, they are therefore undeluded; being those whose ignorance has ceased, they go to that imperishable state. //5//
Madhusūdana:
Having first explained the search [for the self], he speaks of the other limbs of the Vaiṣṇava state in the verse beginning with "nirmāṇa.
*Māna* is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), that is, pride.
Delusion (*moha*), however, is non-discrimination or error; they are "free from pride and delusion" (*nirmānamohāḥ*) because they have emerged from those two,
or because pride and delusion have departed from them.
That is to say, they are free from the lack of discrimination regarding the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

Having conquered the fault of attachment means that they are devoid of passion and aversion even when confronted with the pleasant and the unpleasant. Being "constantly focused on the inner self" (*adhyātma-nityāḥ*) means being intent upon perceiving the nature of the Supreme Self.
"Those whose desires have turned away" means those from whom sensual enjoyments—the objects of desire—have ceased, specifically and without remainder.
The meaning is that they have abandoned all actions by means of solitude (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*).
"By dualities" refers to cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and so forth, which are designated as pleasure and pain because they are the causes of pleasure and pain.

In the alternative reading *sukha-duḥkha-nāmakaiḥ sukha-duḥkha-saṅgaiḥ*, [it means] those who are liberated from— that is, have abandoned— the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) which are called "pleasure and pain" and which possess attachment (*saṅga*), that is, a connection (*sambandha*), with pleasure and pain.

Those who are undeluded, whose ignorance regarding the Self has been dispelled by the perfect knowledge born from the authority of the Vedānta, attain that imperishable state as it has been described. //5//
Viśvanātha:
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of people become and reach that state when devotion to Him exists, he says "nirmāna" and so forth.
"Constantly devoted to the inner self" means those for whom the investigation of the inner self is a constant duty; they are intent upon the contemplation of the Supreme Self. //5//
Baladeva says: Regarding how virtuous persons attain that state when they have surrendered to Him, he says "nirmāna-... and so forth.
*Māna* is the pride born of being honored;
*moha* is false attachment. They are those who have emerged from these two.
Those by whom the defect of attachment—characterized by affection for one's beloved wife and so forth—is conquered;
those for whom there is constant, perpetual inquiry into the inner self regarding the nature of the self and the non-self;

and those who, being capable of enduring them, are liberated from the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, which are designated as "pleasure" and so on because they are the causes of pleasure and pain.
They are undeluded and know the procedure for surrender. //5//
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, reaching which they do not return. //6//
Śrīdhara: He qualifies that very goal which is to be reached with the words "not that.
That state is not illumined by the sun and other luminaries;
having attained it, yogins do not return.
That is my supreme abode, my essential nature.
By this, the objection that it would be subject to insentience or defects such as cold and heat—on the grounds of being an object of illumination like the sun and other luminaries—is refuted. //6//
Madhusūdana:
He specifies that very goal which is to be reached by saying "not that.
That Vaiṣṇava state, having gone to which yogins do not return, is not illumined even by the sun, though it possesses the power to illuminate everything.
Fearing that the moon might be seen as an illuminator even when the sun has set, he says: "not the moon.
Fearing that fire might be seen as an illuminator even when both the sun and the moon have set, he says: "not fire.
The phrase "illuminates" is to be supplied in both instances.

Why is it that the sun and other luminaries lack the capacity to illuminate there? To this he says: "That abode" (*dhāma*) is the light (*jyotis*) which is self-luminous, the illuminator of all inert lights such as the sun and others, the supreme (*paramam*), the most excellent, my own state (*padam*) consisting of the very nature of Viṣṇu.
For indeed, that which is illuminated by another is not capable of illuminating that which illuminates itself.
And so says the Śruti:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire."
"Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (KaṭhU 2.2.15).
By this, it is shown whether that state is to be known or not.

The objection that in the first case there would be the consequence of duality due to dependence on a knower distinct from the object known, and in the second case there would be the consequence of [the Self] being its own human goal, is refuted;

for even while being unobjectifiable (*avedyatva*), it is itself immediately present (*svayam aparokṣatva*). Here, "unobjectifiability" is stated by way of not being illumined by the sun and other such sources, whereas its "self-evident immediacy" will be explained later in the passage beginning, "That splendor which resides in the sun."
Thus, it should be understood that by means of these two verses, the "petal-word" of the Śruti has been explained. //6//
Viśvanātha:
In response to the inquiry as to what that state is like, he says, "Not that...
The sense is that it is free from the suffering of heat, cold, and so forth, and is self-luminous.
That is my supreme abode—the most excellent, non-material, supersensuous splendor that illumines everything.
As it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"That supreme Brahman divides the entire universe."
"O Bhārata, you should know that this dense radiance is mine alone. Thus it is said:
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, so how could this fire?"
Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
And this is also established by such scriptural passages as [KaṭhU 2.2.15]. //6//
Baladeva: He distinguishes the goal that is to be reached by saying "not that.
That which, having gone there, one does not return from—that is my own abode, my supreme and glorious essential nature.

Even the sun and other luminaries, though they illuminate everything, do not illumine or reveal that [reality], for there is the Vedic scripture beginning with, "The sun does not shine there. The meaning is this: I alone—whose form is self-luminous consciousness, who am the Lord of Lakṣmī, and who am not revealed by the sun and others but rather reveal them myself—am the one signified by the word *pada* (the Goal), and I am attainable by those who have surrendered (*prapanna*). //6//
In this world of living beings, an eternal portion of My very self becomes the individual soul; it draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature. (7)

Śrīdhara: Now, one might raise this objection: "If those who have reached Your abode do not return, then—given the scriptural texts such as 'Having attained the Sat, they do not know that they have attained the Sat'—everyone would attain the Reality at the time of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution.
Who, then, would remain a transmigrating soul? Anticipating this, [the Lord] shows who the transmigrating soul is by means of five verses beginning with "Of Me alone... (mamaiva).
This eternal portion of My very self, which has become a living soul (jīva) due to ignorance and is perpetually known as a transmigrating being,

draws back those senses— of which the mind is the sixth— from their state of dissolution in primordial nature (prakṛti) during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, for the sake of experiencing the cycle of worldly existence in the realm of living beings.
And this is intended to include the organs of action and the vital breath (prāṇa) as well.
The meaning is this: it is true that even in deep sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution, because all living beings whatsoever are portions of Me, there is indeed attainment of Me;
nevertheless, for one who is veiled by ignorance and accompanied by latent impressions (anuśaya), the dissolution occurs in Me along with primordial nature (prakṛti), but not in the pure [Self].
Thus it has been said: "From the unmanifest, all manifest beings emerge," and so forth.

And therefore, when the ignorant one goes out again toward saṃsāra, he draws back the senses—which serve as his own limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and which remain dissolved within primordial nature (prakṛti).
But for the wise, because of the attainment of their pure essential nature, there is no return. //7//
Madhusūdana:
It has been stated more than once that the ultimate essential nature of the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman;
all of this will be established by the subsequent portion of the text.

In this regard, it is established by the half-verse beginning with "A portion of My very self" (Gītā 15.7a) that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of Brahman, once it has attained its true nature through the cessation of ignorance, there is no falling away from it;

however, because ignorance accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of all effects persists during deep sleep, the soul returns again to transmigratory existence, as is established by the half-verse beginning with "The six, with the mind as the sixth" (Gītā 15.7b).

Then, although he does not in reality transmigrate, for one who has attained transmigration through *māyā* and has been made to identify with the body by those of dull intellect, his distinction from the body is established by the half-verse beginning with "The body" (Gītā 15.8).
By the verse beginning with "The ear, the eye" (Gītā 15.9), however, his distinction from the senses is established as their respective activators within their own respective objects.

In response to the doubt— “Why do all not perceive that which is thus distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, since it is one's own self-nature at the time of departure and the like?”— the answer is stated in the verse beginning with “As he departs” (Gītā 15.10a): those whose minds are distracted by sense objects do not perceive him, even though he is fit for perception.
The phrase "those who possess the eye of knowledge see it" is explained by the half-verse beginning with "striving yogins" (Gītā 15.11a).
The phrase "the deluded do not perceive it" is explained by the half-verse beginning with "even though striving" (Gītā 15.11b). This is the connection between these five verses.
Now, we shall explain the words starting with "my" (mama).

Even though I, the Supreme Self, am partless, a portion is imagined through *māyā*—like the sun reflected in water or the sky within a jar—possessing a false sense of division. This "portion," as it were, exists in the world of living beings (*jīva-loka*) within *saṃsāra*; and by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of sustaining the vital breaths, it becomes the individual soul (*jīva*), appearing as an agent, an enjoyer, and one who wanders. Thus, having attained a false reputation, it is nevertheless eternal (*sanātana*) and constant, because in reality its nature is that of the Supreme Self even when delimited by adjuncts.
Therefore, it is logical that upon attaining their own true nature, Brahman, through the cessation of ignorance and the like, they do not return from there.

To explain how one who has become thus returns from deep sleep, he says: those five sense organs called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, with the mind as the sixth—these are the instruments (*liṅga*) of the Self (*indra*), serving as the means for perceiving objects. When the karma that produces experience in the waking and dreaming states is exhausted, they abide in *prakṛti*—that is, they remain in a subtle form within ignorance (*ajñāna*). Then, when the karma that produces experience in the waking state arises again...

The meaning is that, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs for the sake of enjoyment, [the intellect] draws forth [the senses] from primordial nature (prakṛti) through ignorance, manifesting them with the capacity to grasp sense objects.
Therefore, the point is that even though there is no return [to bondage] through knowledge, a return due to ignorance is not logically untenable. //7//
Viśvanātha:
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of individual soul (*jīva*) transcends *saṃsāra* through devotion to You and attains Your state, he says, "A portion of My very self.
As it is stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "He is held to be of two kinds: one's own portion (*svāṃśa*) and a divided portion (*vibhinnāṃśa*)."
The individual soul (*jīva*) is thus a distinct portion [of the Self].
That eternal and constant being, while in a state of bondage, draws toward itself those senses—of which the mind is the sixth—which reside within *prakṛti*, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
He draws them by means of the conceit of ownership, thinking "these are mine," as if pulling a foot-iron or a chain. //7//
Baladeva: Now, in response to the inquiry as to who that individual soul (jīva) is who attains His state through devotion to You, He says, "Of Me alone.
The individual soul is indeed a portion of Me, the Lord of all.
But it does not belong to an Īśvara such as Brahmā or Rudra;
and he is eternal and constant,
not something imagined like the space within a jar.

And that [jīva], situated within the phenomenal world (prapañca) of the realm of living beings, draws toward itself the senses—the ear and so forth—with the mind as the sixth; it carries them away like fetters on the feet.
As to what they are like, he says: "situated in nature" (prakṛti-sthāni), meaning they are effects of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is a transformation of nature (prakṛti).
In this regard, it should be understood that the mind is the effect of the sāttvika ego-sense, while the ear and the other senses are the effects of the rājasa ego-sense.

It is indicated that one who, through surrender to the Blessed One, is freed from the instruments of material nature and has gone to the world of the Blessed One, dwells taking refuge in the Blessed One, distinguished by the bodily instruments of the devotees as if they were ornaments— [as it is said]: "He, indeed, this one established in Brahman,
having cast off this mortal body and attained identity with Brahman, sees through Brahman, [hears] through Brahman..."
For the Mādhyandinīya Śruti states: "He hears this entire Veda and experiences it all," and the Smṛti says:
"Wherein all persons dwell as embodiments of Vaikuṇṭha," and so forth;
thus, there exists a spiritual form (cid-vigraha) perfected by the will of the Blessed Lord.

As for those who assert that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman— either like the space within a jar or like the space within water due to being delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

or because of the destruction of its reflection therein— and that upon the destruction of the internal organ, the part that is the individual soul attains the state of pure Brahman, just as the respective spaces become pure space when the jar or the water is destroyed; [this is their view].
That is not the essence; it is the individual soul, which is a portion of Me.
This is because it would contradict the statement that [the Self] is eternal (*sanātana*),
and because both doctrines concerning limitation and so forth have been rejected in the passage, "As the embodied one in this [body]" (Gītā 2.12).
However, its identity [with Brahman] should be understood through similarity to a reflection, as determined by the section on water (*ambuvad-adhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, the soul's status as a subordinate part of Brahman and its being a portion of Brahman are established; for this "being a portion" (aṃśatva) is seen in such cases as "the orb of Venus is a hundredth part of the lunar orb," where it is said that being a portion consists in being a single part of one and the same substance. Indeed, Brahman is the one substance possessing power, while the power of Brahman is [the soul].

"Know that there is another nature of Mine, higher than this, which is the soul (jīva-bhūta)" (Gītā 7.5); because of this previous statement, the individual soul is a portion of That from one part thereof. //7//
Whatever body the Lord assumes and whatever [body] He departs from,
He goes taking these [senses] with Him, just as the wind carries fragrances from their sources. (15.8)
Śrīdhara: Having drawn them forth, what does he do?
To this he says, "the body.

Whenever the Lord—the master of the body and its adjuncts—attains another body by the power of karma, and from whichever body he departs, then, having taken these [elements] from the previous body, he enters that other body.
He proceeds correctly.
Even while the body exists and the senses are engaged in perception, there is this illustration:
just as the wind goes forth after grasping subtle fragrant particles from their source—such as flowers—from their location, so it is in this case. //8//
Madhusūdana:
At this time, it is said that the body "draws [the soul]";
when the Lord—the master of the aggregate of the body and senses, namely the *jīva*—departs, that is, goes out externally, then from that [point].

"Then, departing from the body, it draws along the senses with the mind as the sixth"—this is the first syntactic connection of the second quarter [of the verse], because the act of going occurs subsequent to the departure. It does not merely draw them along; [it also acts as follows]...
But whenever he acquires another body from the previous one, he departs—indeed, he goes away completely, without returning—taking these senses, with the mind as the sixth.

Even while the body still exists, there is an illustration for this grasping of the senses: just as the wind blows, taking subtle portions consisting of fragrance from their source, such as flowers and other places. //8//
Viśvanātha:
In response to the inquiry as to what one does after drawing those [subtle elements] forth, he says: "the body.
That which is the gross body, which one obtains by the power of karma—

And from whichever body the Lord— the individual soul (jīva), the master of the body, senses, and so forth— departs or issues forth, he goes away taking these very senses along with the subtle elements,
just as the wind [carries] fragrances from their source, such as garlands, sandalwood, and the like.
The meaning is that, just as [the wind] carries fragrances along with its subtle particles and moves elsewhere, so it is here.
Baladeva says: It was stated that [the soul], while situated in the world of living beings, draws forth the senses;
he establishes that point with the verse beginning "the body."

The Lord is the master of the body and the senses; whenever the individual soul (jīva) acquires a new body different from its previous one, or when it departs from the body it has acquired, it then takes these senses along with the subtle elements of matter and goes forth, just as the wind, having taken up fragrances from the interior of a flower, moves elsewhere. Thus it is. //8//
Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose, as well as the mind, this [self] experiences the objects of the senses. (9)
Śrīdhara: Showing those very senses and stating for what purpose he goes having grasped them, he says "the ear" and so forth.
The external senses, such as the ear, and the internal organ, the mind—presiding over and depending upon these, this individual soul (jīva) experiences objects such as sound. //9//
Madhusūdana:
Showing those very senses and stating for what purpose he goes having grasped them, he says "the ear," etc.:
"The ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose."

And by virtue of the word "ca" (and), this individual soul (jīva), having presided over—that is, having depended upon—the organs of action, the vital breath (prāṇa), and the mind as the sixth, enjoys—that is, experiences—the objects such as sound and the rest. //9//
Viśvanātha:
To the question of what he does after going there, he says "the ear" and so forth.
Having presided over—that is, having taken recourse to—the sense organs such as the ear and the mind, he experiences objects such as sound. //9//
Baladeva: Having taken those [senses], for what purpose does he go? To this he says: "the ear" and so forth.
Presiding over—that is, depending upon—the ear and other senses together with the mind, this individual soul (jīva) experiences objects such as sound and the rest.
The meaning is that the mention of "that" (the self) is for the sake of that [purpose].
From the word "and" (ca), it is to be understood that [the self] presides over the five organs of action and the vital breaths as well. //9//
Whether it is departing, or remaining, or even enjoying experiences while endowed with the qualities, the deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it. (15.10)

Śrīdhara: Now, why do all people not perceive such a Self as distinct from the aggregate of cause and effect? To this he says: "departing," etc. The deluded do not perceive the individual soul (jīva)—whether it is departing from one body to another, or remaining in that very same body, or experiencing sense objects, or endowed with the qualities (guṇas) and joined with the senses and so forth.
They do not look [with physical eyes];
those for whom knowledge alone is the eye, being discerning, see. //10//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, even that which pertains to the body—namely, the yoga of vision—is [described] as "departing from the body. Departing means going to another body from the previous one.
Whether remaining in that very body or experiencing objects such as sound and so forth,
it is "endowed with qualities," meaning it is accompanied by the qualities consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Thus, although this Self is capable of being seen in all states, the deluded do not perceive It because their minds are drawn away by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoying objects seen and unseen, rendering them incapable of discriminating between the self and the non-self.
"Alas, what a tragedy!"—thus the Blessed One expresses compassion for the ignorant.
But those who possess the eye of knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are discriminative—they alone see It. //10//
Viśvanātha:
Now, we do not perceive any such distinction as to from which body one departs, or in which body one remains, or how one experiences enjoyments while staying therein.
To this he says: "departing," that is, exiting from the body.

The deluded—those lacking discrimination—perceive it as remaining within the body, as existing externally, as enjoying sense objects, and as endowed with the qualities (guṇas) and accompanied by the senses and so forth; whereas those possessing the eye of knowledge are the discriminating ones. //10//
Baladeva: Thus, he says "ut" (out) to show that the undiscriminating do not perceive that Self which is capable of being experienced as residing within the body.

Whether it is departing from the body, or remaining right there, or staying and enjoying sense-objects—being "endowed with qualities" (*guṇānvitam*), meaning joined with pleasure, pain, and delusion, or with the senses and so forth—the Self is indeed capable of being experienced; yet the deluded, whose eye of knowledge has long been obscured, do not perceive it.
But those whose eye is the knowledge of discernment see Him;
they experience Him as distinct from the body and other such things. //10//
Yogis who strive perceive Him established within themselves; yet those of unrefined self, though they strive, do not perceive Him, being devoid of wisdom. (15.11)
Śrīdhara: This Self is difficult to know because even among those who possess discrimination (*vivekin*), some perceive It while others do not; thus he says, "Those who strive.
Some yogis, striving through meditation and other means, perceive this Self situated within the body as distinct.

However, those whose selves are unrefined—meaning those with unpurified minds—and who are consequently "unconscious" or dull-witted, do not perceive It despite making efforts through the study of the scriptures and so forth. //11//

Madhusūdana explains the statement "those with the eye of knowledge see" as follows: "yatantaḥ" (striving). Only those yogis who strive—exerting themselves through meditation and other means—see this Self, which is situated within their own intellect (*ātman*) and reflected therein.
The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Viśvanātha explains that even those who strive—yet whose selves are unrefined, meaning whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have not been purified by sacrifices and other such acts, and who are therefore "unconscious" (*acetasaḥ*), i.e., devoid of discrimination (*viveka*)—do not see this; thus, "the deluded do not perceive it" is a further clarification of that point.
And since those who are discerning are indeed striving yogis, he says "striving" (yatantaḥ);
whereas those of unrefined self are those whose minds are impure. //11//
Baladeva: Explaining the statement that "those with the eye of knowledge see," he describes its difficulty of being known by the word "striving.
Some yogis, striving and practicing means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, perceive this Self situated within the self, which is the body.

Yet others, though striving, do not perceive it because they are unrefined—meaning their minds are impure—and thus they are of dull intellect, lacking the awakened wisdom of discrimination. The meaning is that the reality of the Self is difficult to know. //11//
That splendor which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in the fire— know that splendor to be mine. 15.12

Śrīdhara: Thus, by the verse beginning with "The sun does not illuminate that," the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord has been described, and the non-return of those who have attained it has been stated.
In that context, having raised the doubt as to the non-existence of transmigrating beings, the true nature of the transmigrator as distinct from the body and so forth has been shown.
Now, with four verses beginning with "That which," he describes that very form of the Supreme Lord as possessing infinite power:
know that all this light—of various kinds, situated in the sun and other sources, and which illumines the universe—is indeed My own. (12)
Madhusūdana:
Now, that state which even the sun and other luminaries, though capable of illuminating everything, are unable to illuminate;
reaching which those seeking liberation do not return again to saṃsāra; and following the distinctions of whose limiting adjuncts...
Individual souls, like the spaces within jars and so forth, are merely imagined portions of the one Space (ākāśa) and experience the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) as something false.

In order to demonstrate that this state is the Self of all and the locus of all worldly transactions— and thus to explain what was previously stated in the verse "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27)— the Blessed Lord speaks the word *yat* in these four verses, providing a summary of His own manifestations (*vibhūti*).

By the passage beginning with, "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire" (KaṭhU 2.2.15), the meaning of the Śruti—namely, "Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (KaṭhU 2.2.15)—is explained. That splendor which resides in the sun, consisting of consciousness, that light which is in the moon, and that light which is situated in fire, [illumines] the entire world.
Know that this light which illumines is mine, belonging to me.

Although the light consisting of consciousness is equal in all things, both stationary and moving, nevertheless, because of the excellence of the *sattva* quality, the sun and other luminaries possess a superior degree of excellence; thus, the light of consciousness is more extensively manifest in them alone, and for this reason they are distinguished by such expressions as "that which resides in the sun" and so forth.
Just as, although the proximity to a face is equal, the face does not appear in wood, walls, and the like,

but appears with varying degrees of clarity in mirrors and other objects according to their relative transparency— likewise, by first stating "the light residing in the sun" and then saying "know that light to be mine," the use of the term "light" indicates that which resides in the sun and so forth.
Luminosity is light; it is a white and brilliant form capable of illuminating others, which illumines the entire world—that is, all material objects.
Thus, a second meaning should also be understood for the sake of describing His manifestations: "Know that luminosity, whether in the moon or in fire, which illumines the world, to be Mine."
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "Know that to be mine," without the inclusion of the term *tejas*; such is the intended meaning. //12//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, regarding whatever object is to be attained by the bound soul (jīva) during its state of bondage, [the Lord] says in three verses beginning with "That which... that He Himself, existing as the sun, moon, and so forth, provides assistance.

The very light situated in the sun, having risen in the morning from the mountain of sunrise, exists for the purpose of setting in motion the karma—the means for the experienced and unexperienced enjoyment—of the individual soul (jīva).
And whatever illuminates the world thus in the moon and in fire, all that is indeed mine;
the meaning is that I myself exist under the names of the sun and so forth.
The sense is that the various manifestations of those [luminaries] are merely the manifestation of my own splendor. //12//

Baladeva: Now, with the thought that "I alone am the means for the enjoyment and liberation of the individual soul (jīva), who is a portion of Me, who is attached to worldly existence, and who desires liberation," He says "That which... in four verses.
Know that the splendor which resides in the sun, and that which resides in the moon and in fire, and which illuminates the entire world—that splendor is mine; it belongs to Me.
When the sun has risen and fire has blazed, actions whose means of enjoyment were previously unseen are accomplished;

furthermore, the destruction of darkness and dullness and other such factors become causes of happiness. When the moon has risen, the nourishment of medicinal herbs, the alleviation of heat, and the enjoyment of moonlight likewise come to pass. Thus, that specific energy which accomplishes each of these is the manifestation of my own energy—this is the meaning. //12//
And entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital power;
and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all plants.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the earth" (gām):
having presided over the earth with my own power and strength, I alone sustain all moving and unmoving beings.
Having become the Soma consisting of essence, I alone cause all herbs, such as rice and the like, to grow. //13//
Madhusūdana:

Furthermore, having entered the earth (gām) in the form of the deity Earth and having solidified the earth with my own vigor and strength—making it as firm as a handful of dust—I alone support all beings, which are the objects resting upon the earth;
otherwise, the earth would crumble like a handful of sand or sink downwards.

From the wording of the mantra, "By whom the formidable heaven and the earth were made firm" (Yajurveda 1.8.5; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.1.8), and from the verse, "He supported the earth" (Ṛgveda 8.7.3.1), it is the Blessed One himself who is spoken of as having attained the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.

Moreover, having become Soma—the essence of taste whose nature consists of all flavors—I alone nourish all the herbs born upon the earth, such as rice and barley, making them full of nourishment and sweet with flavor. //13//
Viśvanātha:
Having entered and presided over the earth (gāṃ) by my own power (ojasā), I alone sustain all beings, both moving and unmoving.
Likewise, having become the moon (soma), which consists of the essence of nectar, I alone cause all plants, such as rice and others, to grow. 13.

Baladeva says: "By the earth"—meaning the earth, which is like a handful of dust—I enter it by my own power (*ojas*), that is, by my own capacity, and having made it firm, I support all beings, both stationary and moving.
And the Vedic mantra also speaks thus: "By whom the formidable heaven and the earth were made firm" (Ṛgveda 8.7.3.1).
The implication is that otherwise, this earth would crumble like a handful of sand or sink down.
Likewise, having become the Moon, the essence of nectar consisting of rasa, I alone nourish all herbs— the entirety of rice and other grains—
making them full of various sweet flavors.

And so, for the living being situated in the world of earth, having fashioned various pleasure grounds such as palaces, gardens, and ponds, I alone am the means for that person who enjoys various flavors therein.
Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire and taking refuge in the bodies of living beings, I, conjoined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, digest the fourfold food. (15.14)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [it is said]: "I am He.

Indeed, I, the Lord, having become Vaiśvānara—the digestive fire within the bodies of living beings—enter therein together with the prāṇa and apāna breaths which kindle it, and [consume] that which is eaten, chewed, licked, and sucked by those living beings.
I cook four kinds of food.
Among them, that which is eaten by being repeatedly chewed with the teeth, such as cakes and the like, is called *bhakṣya*.
But that which is swallowed after being merely stirred with the tongue, such as milk-rice and the like, is called *bhojya*.
That which, having been placed upon the tongue, is gradually swallowed while being tasted for its flavor—such as molasses and the like when liquefied—is *lehya* (the lickable).

That which, however, is squeezed with the teeth and so forth, whereby the essential part is swallowed and the remainder is discarded—such as a stalk of sugarcane and the like—is *coṣya* (the suckable). Thus, there are four varieties of this [food]. //14//
Madhusūdana said:
Furthermore, "I am"—
that is, I myself, as the Lord Vaiśvānara, having become the digestive fire within the stomach, [am] this Vaiśvānara fire which is here within.

As established by such scriptural passages as, "That by which this food is cooked in the person— that which is eaten here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9.1)— I, being present and having entered within the bodies of all living beings, joined with and kindled by the prāṇa and apāna breaths which inflame it, cook the fourfold food eaten by living beings: that which is chewed, that which is sucked, that which is licked, and that which is drunk.
There are two types: that which is licked and that which is sucked.
Among these, that which is eaten by repeatedly biting with the teeth, such as cakes and the like, is called *bhakṣya*.
However, that which is swallowed after being stirred only with the tongue, such as soup, boiled rice, and the like, is called *bhojya*.

That which, having been placed upon the tongue, is swallowed by tasting its flavor—such as molasses, *rasālā*, *śikhariṇī*, and other substances that have become somewhat liquefied—is called *lehya* (the lickable). However, that which is pressed with the teeth, the flavorful portion of which is swallowed while the remainder is discarded, such as stalks of sugarcane and the like, is called *coṣya* (the suckable); this is the distinction. Furthermore, for one who meditates on the eater as Vaiśvānara Agni and the food to be eaten as Soma—thus perceiving both of these as the entirety of Agni and Soma—there is no taint from the defects of food.

Viśvanātha: Vaiśvānara is the digestive fire in the stomach; accompanied by the prāṇa and apāna breaths which kindle it, [it consumes] the fourfold food: that which is chewed (bhakṣya), that which is eaten (bhojya), that which is licked (lehya), and that which is sucked (coṣya).
Chewing food (bhakṣya) consists of things to be bitten with the teeth, such as roasted chickpeas and the like; eating food (bhojya) consists of sweetmeats (modaka) and the like.
Licked food (lehya) consists of molasses and the like; sucked food (coṣya) consists of sugarcane stalks and the like. //14//
Baladeva says "I" to show that He alone is the cause of the digestion of the objects of enjoyment, such as food and so forth.
Having become Vaiśvānara— the gastric fire— and having entered the bodies and bellies of all living beings,
and being joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths which kindle it, I [digest] the fourfold food eaten by them.
"I cook food; I bring it to digestion.
And the Śruti says likewise: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed that which is within the person, by whom this food is digested," and so forth.

Accordingly, the author of the Sūtras states: "Because of [the mention of] sound and so forth, and because of abiding within," and so on, declaring that I myself am the gastric fire and the body, being its benefactor.

And food is of four kinds, distinguished as that which is to be chewed (bhakṣya), that which is to be eaten (bhojya), that which is to be licked (lehya), and that which is to be sucked (cūṣya). That which is bitten with the teeth, such as chickpeas, cakes, and the like, is called both "chewable" (carvya) and "to be chewed" (bhakṣya).
Food to be eaten (*bhojya*) consists of sweetmeat balls, boiled rice, soup, and so forth;
food to be licked (*lehya*) consists of milk-rice, molasses, honey, and so forth;
food to be sucked (*cūṣya*) consists of ripe mangoes, stalks of sugarcane, and so forth.
It should be understood that the statement of the identity between Soma and Vaiśvānara is due to [the latter] being pervaded by the former. //14//
And I am seated within the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
And by all the Vedas, I alone am to be known;
I am indeed the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas. 15.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, I have entered the heart of every living being perfectly in the form of the inner controller (antaryāmin).
Therefore, for this very reason, the memory of past objects arises in all living beings solely from Me;
likewise, knowledge born from the contact between the sense objects and the senses arises from Me.
And there occurs the concealment and the forgetting of those two [names and forms].
Furthermore, by means of all the Vedas, in the form of this or that deity and so forth, I alone am the one to be known;
I am the author of the Vedānta and the one who sets its tradition in motion.
The meaning is: "I am the Guru who bestows knowledge";
and I alone am the knower of the Vedas, that is, the knower of the meaning of the Vedas. //15//

Madhusūdana: Furthermore, being the Self (*ātman*) of the entire multitude of living beings—from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—I am seated within the heart, that is, in the intellect (*buddhi*), according to the Vedic revelation: "He entered here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), and also:
"Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

Therefore, for the multitude of living beings, memory— which is a mental function directed toward objects experienced in this life according to their respective capacity— and likewise for yogis, that which is directed toward objects experienced in other births,
as well as knowledge arising from the contact between the senses and their objects,
and even that which pertains to objects remote in space and time for yogis, all proceed from Me alone.
Thus, for those whose minds are distracted by desire, anger, grief, and the like, the removal of such distractions as well as the loss of memory and knowledge arises from Me alone.

Having thus described My nature as the individual soul (*jīva*), He speaks of My nature as Brahman: "By all the Vedas, even those that reveal deities such as Indra, I alone am to be known, because I am the Self of all.
They speak of Me as Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Moreover, he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa;
being one, the sages call him many—
they speak of him as Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
This is because of the wording of the mantra, "Ṛk 2.3.22.6," and because of the Śruti, "For he alone is indeed all the gods.
He is the author of the Vedānta and the one who set in motion the tradition of the meaning of the Vedānta, appearing in the form of Veda-vyāsa and others.

It is not merely this much; I am indeed a knower of the Vedas, and I alone am the one who understands the meaning of the entire Veda—consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas and comprising the sections on ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa), meditative worship (upāsanā-kāṇḍa), and knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa).
Therefore, it has been rightly said: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27), and so forth. //15//
Viśvanātha:
Just as the digestive fire resides within the stomach, even so I, in the form of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), am seated in the heart of all that is moving and unmoving;
for from me alone, from that very principle of intellect, arises the recollection of objects previously experienced.
Likewise, there occurs the knowledge born from the contact of the senses with their objects, as well as *apohana*, which is the disappearance of memory and cognition.

Having stated that [the Vedas] are beneficial to the individual soul (*jīva*) during its state of bondage, he now states their benefit even regarding that which is to be attained in the state of liberation, using the words "by the Vedas" (*vedaiḥ*).

Since I alone am the author of the Vedanta through the agency of Veda-Vyāsa, and since I alone am the knower of the Vedas and the knower of the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas, the meaning is that no one other than me knows the meaning of the Vedas. //15//
Baladeva says: "I alone am the cause of knowledge and ignorance for living beings," as expressed in the words "of all" (sarvasya).

Within the hearts of those two—Soma and Vaiśvānara—and within the entire multitude of living beings, I alone am seated as the controller in that body which is the source of the arising of knowledge, the cause of all activity.
As it is said: "He has entered within, the ruler of people" (TaittA 3.11).
Because of such scriptural declarations as these,

it follows that from Me alone arises for everyone memory— the knowledge that reconnects with objects previously experienced— as well as the cognition produced by the contact of the senses with their objects;
and the removal and the loss of both of these also proceed from Me.
Thus it was said by Uddhava: "Indeed, knowledge regarding living beings is derived from you; therein lies their power.
Having thus stated that he is the means for worldly enjoyment, he speaks of him as the means for liberation with the words "by the Vedas" (vedaiś ca).
By all the Vedas in their entirety, I alone—the Lord of all, the omnipotent Kṛṣṇa—am to be known.
"He who is sung of by all the Vedas"—so says the Śruti.
Here it should be understood that this is [achieved] indirectly through the Karma-kāṇḍa, but directly through the Jñāna-kāṇḍa.
If one asks, "How is this to be understood?", he says in response: "I alone am the author of the Vedānta."
The culmination of the Vedas is the determination of their meaning, and I alone am its author in the form of Bādarāyaṇa.
Thus the author of the Sūtras has declared through such passages as "But that [Brahman is known] from the harmony [of the texts]" (VS 1.1.4).
Now, one might object: "But others explain the meaning of the Vedas differently."

Regarding this, Bādarāyaṇa said: "I alone am the knower of the Vedas"—that is, "I alone am the one who knows the meaning of the Vedas. Whatever meaning I have determined is indeed the meaning of the Vedas; anything other than that is merely a manifestation of delusion.
Furthermore, since the reality of the Lord of All, the bestower of liberation, is not understood through the Vedas [in their literal sense], I alone am the means to liberation. (15)

There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (the unchanging) is called the imperishable. //16//
Śrīdhara: Now, with the three verses beginning with "Two," He reveals His own supreme nature, which was previously described as "that supreme abode of Mine.
Two well-known persons exist in the world, namely the perishable (kṣara) and the imperishable (akṣara).
Of these, the one called the perishable person consists of all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects, that is, all bodies.
Because the world, lacking discrimination, commonly identifies the person (*puruṣa*) with the body alone—
just as one speaks of a "pile" meaning a "pile of stones"—
the conscious enjoyer is called *kūṭastha* (immovable), because he remains unchanging even while bodies perish, like a mountain.
But that is called the Imperishable Person by those possessed of discernment. //16//
Madhusūdana:
