Having thus described the Self as conditioned by adjuncts (*sopādhika*), the Blessed Lord out of compassion teaches Arjuna the unconditioned, pure Self (*nirupādhika śuddha ātmā*)—which is free from the two adjuncts of effect and cause denoted by the terms "the Perishable" (*kṣara*) and "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*)—in three verses beginning with "These two... (*dvāv imau*).

In this world of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), there are these two distinct groups of persons who, by virtue of being conditioned by the adjuncts of personhood (*puruṣopādhi*), are designated by the term "person" (*puruṣa*). Which two? He says: "The Perishable and the Imperishable. That which perishes is the "Perishable" (*kṣara*); it is the perishable, the aggregate of effects, which is one "person.

That which does not perish is the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*); it is devoid of destruction, the seed of origin for the person called the Perishable, namely the Lord’s power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), which is the second "person."
The Blessed Lord himself explains those two persons: "The perishable" (*kṣara*) refers to all beings, meaning the entire aggregate of effects;
"the immutable" (*kūṭastha*)—*kūṭa* is synonymous with *māyā*, which is deception consisting in the concealment of the real object and the manifestation of an unreal object;
by that [māyā], in the form of its two powers of veiling and projection.

The Lord, who is established as the immutable (kūṭastha), whose form is the power of māyā, and who has the causal adjunct (kāraṇopādhi), is called "the Imperishable" (akṣara) because He is infinite as the seed of saṃsāra.

Some, however, having designated the category of the insentient by the word "perishable" (kṣara), claim that by the phrase "the immutable is called the imperishable," the individual soul (jīva) is meant;
but that is not correct.

Since it is precisely the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) who is to be established here as the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), it is therefore logical that both the conditioned and unconditioned adjuncts—both of which are insentient—are denoted by the terms "the Perishable" (kṣara) and "the Imperishable" (akṣara). //16//
Viśvanātha:
"Since I alone am the knower of the Vedas, therefore I shall state in brief the essential summary of the meaning of all the Vedas; listen," he says with the three verses beginning with "These two.
In this world, consisting of the fourteen worlds within the insentient phenomenal expansion (jaḍa-prapañca), there exist these two sentient persons (puruṣau).
He explains those two as follows: the *kṣara* (the perishable) is the individual soul (*jīva*), because it "perishes," meaning it falls away from its own true nature;
the *akṣara* (the imperishable) is Brahman alone, because it does not perish from its own true nature. Indeed, O Gārgī, the Brahmins desire to know this very imperishable.
Thus it is from the Śruti;

and from the Smṛti, "The Imperishable (akṣara) is the supreme Brahman," it is seen that the word *akṣara* indeed denotes Brahman. Furthermore, he clarifies the meaning of the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*): all beings are in truth only the one Jīva, [appearing as such] through beginningless ignorance (*anādy-avidyā*).

The meaning is that, having fallen away from its own nature (svarūpa) and being dependent on karma, it becomes the collective self (samaṣṭy-ātmaka) of all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects;
or the singular number is used because of the genus (jāti).
As for the second person, the Imperishable (akṣara), however, is the immutable (kūṭastha); possessing a single, non-deviating nature, it pervades all time.
But that which pervades time by way of a single form is "immutable" (kūṭastha); thus says Amara. //16//
Baladeva: Summarizing the meaning of the Vedas as determined by Bādarāyaṇa, he says, "Two.
From the etymology "that by which reality (tattva) is perceived," *loka* refers to the Veda.
By saying "these two persons are celebrated," it is indicated that they are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "Which two?", he says: "The perishable (kṣara) and so forth.

The perishable is the bound soul (baddha), which, due to the dissolution of the body, exists in manifold states; because of its connection with the single attribute of association with the non-conscious (acid), it is designated as one.

The imperishable (akṣara) is the liberated soul, which, due to the absence of that [dissolution], exists in a single state; because of its connection with the single attribute of dissociation from the non-conscious, it is designated as one.
He clarifies the perishable and the imperishable: all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass are the perishable;
the immutable, abiding in the state of pure being, is the liberated, the imperishable.
The teaching of their identity is to be understood through the reasoning previously stated.
From such passages as "Many [attained perfection] through knowledge and austerity" and "Having resorted to this knowledge," that [number of sages] is plural in count. //16//
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (Paramātman), who, entering the three worlds, sustains them as the imperishable Lord. 15.17
Śrīdhara: He states the purpose for which these two have been characterized with the word "the Supreme" (uttama).
Distinct from these two—the perishable and the imperishable—is the Supreme Person (puruṣa).
He explains this very distinction: he is declared and spoken of by the Vedas as the "Supreme Self" (paramātman).
The meaning is that he is distinct from the perishable, insentient [matter] by virtue of being the Self (ātman),
and distinct from the imperishable, sentient enjoyer by virtue of being the Supreme (parama).
He demonstrates his status as the Supreme Self with the words, "He who [created] the three worlds."
He who is the Lord, whose nature is to rule, and who is immutable and changeless, having entered the entirety of the three worlds, sustains and protects them. //17//
Madhusūdana:

Distinct from these two—the perishable and the imperishable—untouched by the defects of the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the perishable and the imperishable, His nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free; thus He is "the Supreme" (uttama).

The Supreme, the most excellent Person, is indeed other than these two, being absolutely distinct from them; the meaning is that He is a third mass of consciousness, the illuminator of both these masses of insentient matter.

He is called the "Supreme Self" (paramātman) because He is superior to and more excellent than the five selves imagined through ignorance— namely, those consisting of food, vital breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss— and because He is declared to be the unimagined Brahman, the tail, the foundation;
and because He is the inner conscious self of all beings, He is thus called the Supreme Self in the Vedāntas.

The Supreme Self (paramātman)—that is, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all modification and the controller of everything—having entered the three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, that is to say, the entire universe, sustains it by presiding over it through His own power of Māyā; He maintains and nourishes it by providing it with existence and manifestation. Of what nature is He? He is the Imperishable (avyaya), devoid of all change. Such is the construction [of the verse]: He is the Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa) and is declared to be the Supreme Self.
"He is the Supreme Person," according to the Śruti. //17//
Viśvanātha:

Having described Brahman as the object of worship for the knowers (*jñānins*), he speaks of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the object of worship for the yogis, beginning with the word "uttama" (the highest). The particle "tu" (but) indicates its distinction from what preceded it.
And since it has been stated that "the yogi is superior even to the men of knowledge," the excellence of the object of worship is also obtained from the very excellence of the worshipper.

[The Lord] reveals the reality of the Supreme Self: He who is the Lord, whose nature is to rule, being Himself immutable and changeless, pervading the entire three worlds, sustains, supports, and protects them. 17.
Baladeva: He states "the Supreme" (uttama) to explain the purpose for which the two persons were described.
The meaning is that he is distinct from both the perishable and the imperishable, and is not merely one of those two according to their own volition.
In this regard, he cites scriptural authority, saying "the Supreme Self" (paramātman).
He states the quality that constitutes supremacy with the words "yo loka... (He who...).
Furthermore, this sovereignty consisting of the creation and protection of the world does not belong to a bound soul (*baddha-jīva*), because for such a soul, action is impossible;
nor does it belong to a liberated soul (*mukta*), because of the prohibition: "except for the activity of the world" [in the case of the liberated]. //17//
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). 18.18

Śrīdhara: Having spoken thus, he demonstrates his own status as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) through the etymological derivation of his name, beginning with "yasmāt" and so forth. Because I have transcended the perishable (kṣara), which is the category of the insentient, due to being eternally liberated; and because I am superior even to the imperishable (akṣara), which is the category of the sentient, due to being the controller.
Therefore, I am celebrated and renowned in both the world and the Veda as Puruṣottama.
And so says the Śruti: "He alone is the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he governs this entire universe," and so forth. //18//
Madhusūdana:

Now, by means of the etymological explanation of the well-known name *Puruṣottama* for the Lord—who has been described as distinct from both the perishable and the imperishable—the Blessed One reveals Himself, saying, "I am this very Supreme Lord," in the words: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27).
[14.27] "That is My supreme abode" (Gītā 15.6), and so forth—this is stated for the purpose of determining My own majesty as previously described.

Because I, the Supreme Lord, have transcended—that is, gone beyond—the perishable *aśvattha* tree of worldly existence, which consists of Māyā and is subject to destruction due to its nature as an effect; and because I am higher than even the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the unmanifest known as Māyā, I am "the Highest of the High."
He is superior, indeed the most excellent, even to the cause of all things— the seed of the tree of saṃsāra— which is indicated by the word ending in the fifth case (the genitive).

Therefore, because He is superior to the two types of Puruṣas— the perishable and the imperishable— who are designated by the term "Puruṣa" through superimposition, I am celebrated and renowned in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama.

Thus, he is declared in the Veda as "the Supreme Person" (puruṣottama), and this is well-known in the world, as well as in the poetry of the poets, where it is said, for example: "Hari alone is remembered as the Supreme Person.
Out of compassion, He acted like a human being, performed deeds for the sake of others, and revealed His own divine sovereignty to Arjuna.
The majesty of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, whose singular body consists of existence and consciousness, truly does not admit of measure.
Some, having restrained the senses and renounced worldly enjoyment,
strive with pure intellects for yoga toward the infinite and boundless majesty of Nārāyaṇa.
But I, relishing the essence of the nectar, am liberated. //18//
Viśvanātha:

Having described the Supreme Self (paramātman) who is worshipped by yogis, he now speaks of the Blessed Lord (bhagavān) who is worshipped by devotees. While explaining that even in His state as the Blessed Lord, his own essential form as Kṛṣṇa bears the name "Puruṣottama," he declares His absolute supremacy with the words beginning with "yasmāt" (because...).
He has transcended the perishable person, the individual soul (jīvātman), and is even higher than the imperishable Person, the supreme Brahman, the changeless Supreme Self; he is the highest of all,
even among all yogis whose inner self is absorbed in Me.
"He who, endowed with faith, worships Me,
he is considered by Me to be the most disciplined" (Gītā 6.47).
This is because the excellence of the object of worship is obtained precisely through the excellence of the worshiper.

By the inclusion of the word "ca" (and), it is understood that even from the presence of the Blessed Lord Vaikuṇṭhanātha and others, these are but portions and expansions of the Supreme Person; for as the son of Sūta has declared, "But Kṛṣṇa is the Blessed Lord Himself," I am the most excellent.

In this regard, although the single reality whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss is expressed by the terms *brahman*, *paramātman*, and *bhagavān*, there is in fact no difference whatsoever in its essential nature, because there is no duality of essence.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṣṭha-skandha*.

Furthermore, although that [Brahman] is one, it is treated as if distinct because differences are observed among its respective worshippers in terms of both the means of attainment (*sādhana*) and the results attained (*phala*).

To explain: for those who worship Brahman, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), the means for attaining each of these are, respectively, knowledge (*jñāna*), yoga, and devotion (*bhakti*).
In reality, the fruit of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga is liberation alone; however, the fruit of devotion (*bhakti*) is the status of being an attendant endowed with love.

Regarding this, it is said: "Without devotion, even the state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) attained through knowledge and yoga does not shine, if it is devoid of the disposition toward Acyuta" (BhP 1.5.12).
Because of such scriptural observations as, "Indeed, O Infinite One, there have been many yogis," liberation is not attained [by them alone].

Those who worship Brahman—that is, those who worship the Supreme Self—must necessarily practice devotion to the Blessed Lord for the sake of accomplishing their own intended fruit. However, a worshiper of the Blessed Lord does not perform even the worship of Brahman or the worship of the Supreme Self for the sake of accomplishing his own intended fruit.
"Neither knowledge nor detachment generally leads to the highest good in this world" (BhP 11.20.31),
and "Whatever is attained through ritual acts, whatever through austerity, and whatever through knowledge and detachment" (BhP 11.20.32)—
all of this is surpassed by the yoga of devotion to Me.
"My devotee attains heaven and liberation directly, even if he should somehow desire My abode," [BhP 11.20.33].
Indeed, that perfection of means which exists for the four aims of human life— without it, one does not attain those aims.
A person who takes refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
From such statements as these.
Therefore, through the worship of the Bhagavān, all fruits—including heaven, liberation, and divine love—can indeed be attained;

however, through the worship of Brahman or the Paramātman, love and such are not attained. For this very reason, the superiority of the Bhagavān over Brahman and Paramātman is stated even though they are non-different.

Just as, despite non-difference in their nature as light, among the categories of luminosity, lamps, fire, and masses of flame, the mass of fire alone is said to be the best because it removes afflictions such as cold.

Even therein, the supreme excellence belongs to the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone; just as the sun excels even a mass of fire, for he granted the liberation of nirvāṇa— attainable through the ripening of the worship of Brahman— even to his own haters, such as the great sinners Aghāsura, Baka, Jarāsandha, and others.
Therefore, this has been explained exactly as it is by the venerable Śrī Svāmīcaraṇa in the passage, "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman.
And likewise by the venerable feet of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī:
"The form of consciousness and bliss, the essence of the luster of a water-laden cloud, [which is the goal] of the Vedic words..."

"O you who are skilled in undertaking auspicious deeds, worship Him again and again! He has repeatedly manifested incarnations to remove the burden of the earth and to serve as a necklace for the women of Vraja—those whose intellects have reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence. Thus it is said.
From Him whose hand is adorned with a flute, who has the luster of a fresh rain-cloud,
who wears yellow garments, whose lips are like the red bimba fruit,
whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, and whose eyes are like lotuses.
"I know of no reality whatsoever that is superior to Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, the wonderful majesty of Kṛṣṇa is established even by means of authoritative evidence.
Those fools who are unable to endure it have gone to hell.
Since the supreme excellence of Kṛṣṇa has been established by those who have spoken thus, no malice should be displayed toward this commentary on these three verses beginning with "These two.
Homage be to those who possess exclusive knowledge! //18//
Baladeva: Now, he states his own essential nature through the etymological definition of the name Puruṣottama, beginning with the words "yasmāt" (because). He is *uttama*, meaning most excellent.
According to the Nirukta, in the world and in the human scriptures (*pauruṣeya-āgama*), [the term] is so called because "by this, the meaning of the Veda is perceived.
In the Veda, it is said: "This serene being (*samprasāda*), having arisen from this body and having attained the form of the supreme light, manifests in its own true form."

The meaning is that the supreme light, which is celebrated in such passages as "He is the Supreme Person" (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ) and is attained through serene faith (samprasāda), is the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self (paramātman). And in the world:
"But the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), having had his business made known by them..."
The great yogi descended upon Satyavatī from Parāśara.
Thus he is celebrated at the beginning of the Skanda Purāṇa. //18//
O Bhārata, he who, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Supreme Person— he, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being. 19.
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit for one who knows the Lord in such a manner with the word "yaḥ" (he who).
He who, being undeluded and possessing a settled mind in the manner described above, knows Me as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), he worships Me alone with his whole being—that is, in every way.
And consequently, he becomes all-knowing, that is, omniscient. //19//
Madhusūdana:
He states the fruit of knowing the etymological derivation of these names in the verse beginning with "yo mām" (he who [knows] me).
"He who," meaning a certain man who is not deluded, knows me—the Lord—thus, according to the aforementioned etymologies of my names, such as "Kṛṣṇa."

Thus, freed from delusion, he knows that "this is indeed the Lord," the Supreme Person as previously explained; he worships and serves Me. He who knows Me as the All-pervading Self is himself all-knowing. O Bhārata, by means of *bhakti-yoga* characterized by love, with his whole being, he [attains Me].
Therefore, it has been said:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving devotional yoga,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman."
Thus, that [statement from Gītā 14.26] is established;
and as it was said, "For I am the foundation of Brahman," that too is even more thoroughly established.
[I am] the one whose form is consciousness and bliss, whose essence is like the luster of a water-laden cloud, and who am the goal of the words of the Vedas.

O you who are skilled in undertaking auspicious deeds, worship Him again and again; for He repeatedly descends to remove the burden of the earth and to serve as a necklace for the women of Vraja—those whose minds have reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence. 19.
Viśvanātha:
[Objection: "But even when this matter has been established by you, the disputants continue to quarrel;
let them quarrel, for they are deluded by my *māyā*, but the virtuous one is not deluded. To this he says: "He who [knows] me... and so forth.
"Unconfused" means one who is not subject to delusion among speakers;
he alone is omniscient, for even without having studied the scriptures, he knows the true reality of the meaning of all treatises.
The implication is that any other person is indeed thoroughly ignorant and a true fool, despite having studied and mastered all the scriptures.
Likewise, only he who knows thus worships me with his whole being;
the meaning is that others, even if they worship, do not truly worship me. //19//
Baladeva: To illuminate the underlying purport, he states the fruit for one who knows the state of being the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) with the words "He who [knows] me.
Thus, according to the etymological explanation I have given, it is not merely a conventional name like "Aśvakarṇa" and so forth;
he who knows me as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is undeluded.
Having been declared to be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) and thus being free from doubt,
he understands the meaning of these very three verses and is therefore all-knowing,
because the entire Veda has its ultimate purport (tātparya) in that alone.
One who knows my state as the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) worships and serves Me with his whole being, in every way.

My grace—which resides in one who knows the meaning of all the Vedas and who practices all the limbs of devotion—shall be bestowed upon him. However, one who doubts my status as the Supreme Person is ignorant, even if he has studied all the Vedas.
The sense is that even one who worships in every way is not a true devotee. //19//
Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me; having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done. (15.20)
Śrīdhara: He concludes the meaning of the chapter with the word "iti.
In this manner—by this concise method—I have spoken the most secret, the supreme mystery, which is the complete scripture itself;
and not merely this single chapter consisting of twenty verses, O sinless one (anagha), you who are free from calamity.
Therefore, by means of his intellect, the wise man who understands this scripture spoken by Me shall become one who possesses perfect knowledge and shall have fulfilled his duty.
O Bhārata, what more need be said? The sense is that anyone at all has already accomplished their purpose. //20//
Having clearly severed the tree of saṃsāra in the fifteenth chapter, the All-pervading Lord taught the supreme state known as the Yoga of Puruṣottama.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Supreme Person," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:
Now, praising the subject matter of the chapter, he concludes with the words "Thus" (iti).
In this manner, O sinless one, I have spoken here in this chapter this entire scripture, which is the most secret and most profound mystery, in brief.

Having understood this, any other intelligent person who possesses self-knowledge would have accomplished all that is to be done; he would be one for whom no further duty remains, and thus he would be "one who has fulfilled his task. The intended meaning is that whatever must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa born of a distinguished lineage—all that becomes accomplished once the reality of the Blessed Lord is known; otherwise, the duty of anyone is never fully completed.

"O Bhārata, since you are born of a noble lineage and are yourself free from calamity, by virtue of your family and your own qualities, you will realize this and become one who has accomplished his purpose; what more need be said?"—this is the intended meaning. //20//
From Him whose hand is adorned with a flute, who has the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who wears yellow garments, whose lips and lower lip are like the fruit of the Aruṇa bimba,
whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, and whose eyes are like lotuses.
I know no reality whatsoever that is superior to Kṛṣṇa. //1//
The mind, perpetually immersed in the state of eternal bliss, casts off the nature of the mental faculty;
having immediately abandoned the exhaustion of coming and going, it attains the reality that transcends both the supreme and the non-supreme. //2//
The Śaivas, Sauras, Gāṇeśas, Vaiṣṇavas, and worshippers of Śakti—all become composed of that [reality]; I am that Supreme Śiva. //3//
The wonderful majesty of Kṛṣṇa is established even by means of valid cognition;
those fools who are unable to endure it have gone to hell. //4//

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Supreme Person," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha concludes the meaning of the chapter with the words "iti" (thus):
"By these twenty verses, this most secret scripture has been fully declared by me. (20)
By elucidating the categories of the insentient and the sentient,
it has been stated that the meaning of this chapter is that Kṛṣṇa alone possesses supreme excellence.
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary which showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord, this fifteenth chapter has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 15.
Baladeva: With the thought that this should not be disclosed to unworthy recipients (*apātra*), he says "iti" (thus).

Thus, this scripture consisting of three verses, which is in summary form and defines the state of being the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), has been spoken by me to you, my supreme devotee. O sinless one, the intention is that you too must not reveal this to those who are unworthy.
Having understood this, one becomes wise through indirect knowledge;
and having fulfilled one's duty, one becomes a knower through direct realization—thus, the knowledge of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is highly honored. //20//
That person who is distinct from both the bound and the liberated, yet bears those qualities, is the most excellent;
therefore, it follows from the fifteenth [chapter] that such a person is indeed Hari himself.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad. //15//
